result.summary: Apollodorus tells of the children of Coeus and Latona: Asteria becomes Delos, Latona bears Artemis and Apollo, and Apollo takes Delphi and kills Python, Tityus and Marsyas. Artemis kills Orion, whose life and blinding are told, and the section ends with Poseidon's marriage to Amphitrite.

scenes.title: Asteria and Latona at Delos
scenes.summary: Asteria becomes a quail and plunges into the sea, and the island is named for her and later Delos. Hera hunts Latona until she bears Artemis and Apollo there.
scenes.stakes: Latona is hunted by Hera across the earth; Asteria flees Zeus's advances.

scenes.title: Apollo at Delphi; Tityus
scenes.summary: Apollo learns prophecy from Pan, kills Python and takes the oracle. He and Artemis then shoot Tityus, who assaulted Latona, and he is punished in Hades.
scenes.stakes: Apollo risks the oracle's guardian; Latona faces assault by Tityus.

scenes.title: Apollo and Marsyas
scenes.summary: Marsyas, using Athena's discarded pipes, challenges Apollo to a contest. Apollo wins by the lyre trick and flays Marsyas on a pine.
scenes.stakes: Marsyas stakes his life on the contest, as the victor may do as he wishes with the loser.

scenes.title: Orion's blinding and healing
scenes.summary: Orion, son of Poseidon or born of earth, loses his wife Side, is blinded by Oenopion on Chios, and is healed by the sun's rays in the east.
scenes.stakes: Orion loses his sight and his wives, and seeks vengeance.

scenes.title: Orion's death; Poseidon weds
scenes.summary: Poseidon prepares a trap for Oenopion; Dawn carries Orion to Delos; Orion is killed by Artemis for differing reasons. Poseidon marries Amphitrite.

alias_notes.explanation: Older name of Delphi, where Python lived.

notable_quotes.reason: The grim end of Marsyas, a famous tale of hubris punished.

analysis.text: Apollo and Artemis defend their mother and their honor with violence, punishing those who offend the gods.
Apollodorus gathers rival versions, citing Pherecydes, showing a mythographer reconciling many local traditions.

legacy.text: The flaying of Marsyas became a frequent subject in art, including Titian's late painting The Flaying of Marsyas.
Orion became a constellation and appears widely in later literature and astronomy.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus but was probably written in the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: "Amorous advances" means Zeus's attempts to seduce her; she changed into a quail to escape him.
"Intrigue" here means a secret love affair. Hera, Zeus's wife, punished Latona for it.
"Chasm" refers to the cleft in the earth at Delphi, from which the oracle's inspiration was said to come.
"Debauched" means seduced or violated; the sense here is that Zeus had seduced Elare.
Pytho is an older name for Delphi, linked to the slaying of the Python.
"Work his will on the vanquished" means the winner could do whatever he chose to the loser.
Aphrodite punished Dawn because Dawn had slept with Ares, Aphrodite's lover, so Dawn was made to fall in love constantly.
"Quoits" are heavy discs or rings thrown at a mark, here probably a discus-like contest.

context_notes.text: Delphi was the most famous oracle of Greece, later sacred to Apollo, god of prophecy and music.
Tityus's punishment, vultures devouring his liver or heart in Hades, was a famous example of punishment for crimes against the gods.
Hephaestus was the smith god, so his smithy is where Orion finds a boy to guide him.
Amphitrite was a sea goddess, a daughter of Ocean, who became Poseidon's wife.

literary_notes.text: The organ said to be consumed is the seat of lust that drove his crime, so the punishment fits it.
The terms of the contest, in which the victor may do as he pleases, anticipate Marsyas's gruesome fate.
Oenopion's blinding of Orion answers Orion's wooing of Merope with a cruel retaliation.
